Developing a Musical Mind; Series 2 How to Train Your Musical Mind A musical mind is not developed by simply accumulating music lessons. You can take piano lessons for years and still struggle to hear harmony. You can sing in a choir for years and still struggle with pitch. You can read music fluently and still struggle to communicate musical expression. The question, therefore, is not only how much music you practise, but how intentionally you train your musical mind. “You don’t develop a musical mind by only practising what your hands can do. You develop it by training your ears to recognise what your mind wants your hands to produce.” — Victor Adenola Listen actively One of the most powerful ways to develop musical intelligence is through intentional listening. Don’t always listen to music as background sound. Listen for something specific. Choose a song and ask: What instrument carries the melody? What is the bass doing? Where does the harmony change? What happens to the dynamics? How does the singer phrase the lyrics? Where does the drummer create emphasis? What makes the chorus feel different from the verse? Active listening transforms music from something you consume into something you study. https://victoradenola.wordpress.com/2024/10/25/listening-understanding-music-on-a-deeper-level/ Learn by ear Learning music by ear is one of the most effective ways of strengthening musical awareness. Before looking at the notation, try to identify: The melody; rhythm; starting pitch; chord movement; musical patterns; phrase endings; repeated sections. When you learn by ear, you are training the brain to connect what you hear with what you produce. This is valuable for singers, instrumentalists, accompanists, musicians, choir members and music directors. Sing what you hear Even instrumentalists can benefit greatly from singing. Singing helps establish a direct connection between the inner musical idea and the physical production of sound. Try singing scales, intervals, melodies. Sing rhythms using syllables. Sing a musical phrase before playing it on your instrument. If you cannot sing a phrase accurately, it may be worth asking whether you truly hear it internally. Study music theory—but don’t stop there Music theory gives musicians a framework for understanding what they hear and perform. It helps us understand keys, scales, chords, intervals, harmony, rhythm and musical form. But theory should not become a collection of definitions to memorise for an examination. The real question is: Can you recognise what you have studied when you encounter it in real music? Knowing the definition of a modulation is different from actually hearing one. Knowing how to construct a diminished chord is different from recognising its sound and understanding its function. Knowledge becomes musical intelligence when it can be heard, understood and applied. -Victor Adenola Practise with questions Instead of always practising by repetition, practise through observation. After playing a passage, ask : What worked? What did not work? Why? What can I change? What should this phrase communicate? This approach makes practice more intelligent. You stop being someone who simply repeats a passage until the fingers memorise it. You become someone who understands what needs improvement. Study musicians who are better than you Listen to great singers, conductors, instrumentalists and ensembles. But don’t merely admire them – Analyse them. What are they doing? Why does their interpretation work? How do they use dynamics? How do they shape phrases? How do they respond when something unexpected happens? One of the greatest benefits of studying other musicians is that it expands your own musical vocabulary. Develop rhythmic awareness Rhythm is not only about counting. It is about movement and timing. Practise clapping rhythms. Count aloud. Walk to a pulse. Play with a metronome. Practise starting and stopping accurately. Listen to how different musicians sit around the beat. For bands and choirs especially, rhythmic awareness creates unity. Rhythm is a team work and not just one person’s responsibility. https://victoradenola.wordpress.com/2026/09/28/keeping-rhythm-is-everyones-responsibility/ Train yourself to hear relationships Music is relational. The melody relates to the harmony. The rhythm relates to the pulse. The voice relates to the accompaniment. The individual relates to the ensemble. The phrase relates to the larger structure. As your musical mind develops, you begin to stop hearing isolated elements and start hearing the relationship between them. “A trained musician hears more than individual notes; they hear relationships, direction, tension, release and possibility.” — Victor Adenola A simple daily musical-mind exercise You don’t need hours to begin. Try this for 20 minutes : Active listening: Listen to one piece and identify three things you hear. – 5 minutes Ear training: Sing or identify intervals, scales, rhythms or melodies. – 5 minutes Musical analysis: Study a short phrase and identify its structure, harmony, rhythm or dynamics. – 5 minutes Application: Play or sing the phrase while deliberately applying what you discovered. – 5 minutes Over time, this changes the way you approach music. Final Thought The purpose of practice is not simply to make you faster, louder or more accurate. It should also make you more aware. A musician who practises only the physical aspects of music may become technically competent. A musician who trains the ear, mind and body together develops something much deeper. A musical mind . Developing a Musical Mind; Series 1 What Does It Mean to Have a Musical Mind? When we describe someone as “musical,” we often mean that the person sings beautifully, plays an instrument well, keeps good rhythm, or seems naturally gifted. But there is something deeper than technical ability. A musician can play many notes without truly understanding the music. A singer can sing every pitch correctly without communicating the meaning of a song. A choir can learn all the notes and rhythms of a piece and still give a performance that feels lifeless. This is where the idea of a musical mind becomes important. “A musical mind does not merely reproduce sound; it understands what the sound is trying to communicate.” — Victor Adenola So, what is a musical mind? Having a musical mind means developing the ability to hear, understand, imagine, interpret, respond to and communicate music intentionally. It is the ability to listen beyond the obvious. You hear the melody, but you also hear its direction. You hear the rhythm, but you understand its movement. You hear the harmony, but you recognise how it supports the emotional character of the music. You notice dynamics, phrasing, articulation, balance, tone and timing—and you understand how they contribute to the whole musical picture. A musical mind asks questions such as: Why does this phrase begin softly? Where is this melody going? Why does the harmony change here? Should this note be sustained or released? Why does this section feel different? What does the composer or songwriter want the listener to experience? What does this music need from me as a performer? These questions take a musician beyond simply playing or singing notes. Technique is important—but technique is not everything In my years of working as a music director, voice coach and music educator, I have observed that technical training can produce competent performers, but musical thinking produces more complete musicians. A student may learn how to play a chord. The next level is understanding when, how and why to use that chord. A singer may learn how to produce a beautiful tone. The next level is understanding how that tone serves the phrase and the message. A drummer may learn a rhythm. The next level is knowing when that rhythm should lead, support, simplify or create space. That is musical thinking. “The goal of music training is not simply to fill the performer with information, but to develop the ability to make meaningful musical decisions.” — Victor Adenola The musical ear and the musical mind The musical ear and musical mind work together. Your ear helps you detect what is happening. Your mind helps you interpret it. For example, a choir may be singing together but sound disconnected. A musically aware director will not simply say, “Sing louder.” The director may recognise that the real problem is poor vowel alignment, inconsistent entrances, weak breath support, unbalanced sections or unclear phrasing. The ability to diagnose the musical problem and respond appropriately is evidence of a developing musical mind. Musical imagination matters too One of the fascinating aspects of musical development is the ability to hear something internally before producing it externally. Before a conductor raises a hand, they should have some idea of the sound they want. Before a singer begins a phrase, they should have an internal sense of its pitch, tone, direction and expression. Before a pianist plays a passage, the mind should already have an idea of how that passage should sound. This is why musicians should not practise only with their hands and voices. They must also practise with their ears and imagination. A musical mind develops over time Nobody needs to be born a musical genius to develop musical intelligence. Listening develops it. Singing develops it. Playing an instrument develops it. Reading music develops it. Studying theory develops it. Performing develops it. Making mistakes—and learning why they happened—develops it. Teaching others develops it. Conducting develops it. Even listening critically to other musicians can develop it. The important thing is to move from asking: “Can I play or sing this?” to: “Do I understand what I am playing or singing?” And eventually: “Can I communicate it?” That is the journey from musical ability to a musical mind. Final thought A complete musician is not simply someone who has trained the fingers, voice or technical skills. A complete musician has also trained the ear, imagination, understanding and judgement. The instrument produces the sound, but the musical mind gives the sound direction.
